questions.q: List the four varnas in hierarchical order and state the primary occupation prescribed for each in the Dharmasutras.
questions.a: Correct order: Brahmana (study/teach Vedas, perform sacrifices), Kshatriya (warfare, protection, administration), Vaishya (agriculture, pastoralism, trade), Shudra (service to the three higher varnas). A wrong answer (e.g., swapping Vaishya and Shudra occupations, or adding "untouchables" as a fifth varna) reveals confusion between varna and jati, or ignorance of the textual hierarchy.

questions.q: The Rigvedic hymn (Source 6) describes a poet whose father was a physician and mother a grain-grinder. Explain why this challenges the Dharmasutra view of varna as birth-based and occupationally rigid.
questions.a: The hymn shows occupational diversity within one family across generations, implying early Vedic society allowed mobility and did not strictly tie occupation to birth. A wrong answer that claims "this proves varna didn't exist yet" misses the nuance: varna as a theoretical ideal developed later; the hymn illustrates pre-ideal flexibility, not absence of social categories.

questions.q: In the Buddhist story (Source 13), a wealthy Shudra employs Brahmana and Kshatriya servants. Apply the varna model to explain why this scenario is a deliberate critique of Brahmanical claims about purity and hierarchy.
questions.a: The story inverts the ritual hierarchy: economic power (wealth) overrides birth-based status, showing varna distinctions are socially constructed, not natural. A wrong answer that says "Buddhists rejected varna entirely" oversimplifies — they rejected birth-based rigidity but acknowledged social differences; the critique targets the claim that Brahmanas are inherently superior.

questions.q: Analyze how the Satavahana rulers' use of metronymics (e.g., Gotami-puta) and endogamous marriages contradict two specific Brahmanical norms from the Dharmasutras.
questions.a: Satavahanas trace descent through mothers (metronymics) instead of strict patriliny, and marry within gotra (endogamy) instead of exogamy. A wrong answer that dismisses this as "non-Brahmanical influence" fails to recognize that ruling elites selectively adopted Brahmanical symbols (claiming Brahmana status) while maintaining indigenous kinship practices — a strategic negotiation, not simple rejection.

questions.q: Evaluate the historian's claim: "The Dharmasutras reflect the aspirations of Brahmana authors more than the actual organization of society." Use evidence from the Manusmriti's eight forms of marriage and the Satavahana inscriptions.
questions.a: The Manusmriti lists eight marriage forms but only approves four; Satavahanas practiced forms condemned by Brahmanas (endogamy, polygyny). This gap shows the texts are prescriptive, not descriptive. A wrong answer that says "the texts were ignored everywhere" ignores that Brahmanical norms shaped royal rhetoric (e.g., Satavahanas claiming to uphold varna order) even while practices diverged.

questions.q: Construct a 150-word argument: "The four-varna model was a theoretical framework that accommodated, rather than erased, regional diversity." Use the Rigvedic hymn, Buddhist critique, and Satavahana practices as evidence.
questions.a: A strong answer will note: (1) Rigvedic flexibility shows pre-model fluidity; (2) Buddhist dialogue exposes the model's internal contradiction (wealth > birth); (3) Satavahanas simultaneously claim Brahmana status and violate exogamy, proving the model was a negotiable idiom. A weak answer merely lists examples without linking them to the "accommodation" thesis.

Fill in the blank: Imagine you find an old family diary that lists "rules for each family member" — but you know real life didn't ______ those rules exactly.
What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: The student can explain the prescribed occupations and ritual hierarchy of the four varnas as laid out in the Dharmasutras, contrast this ideal with evidence of flexibility (Rigvedic hymn, Buddhist critique, Satavahana practices), and analyze why the prescriptive model does not match complex social realities.
